standard.title: Government institutions and democracy
standard.description: the key institutions of Australia's system of government, how it is based on the Westminster system, and the key values and beliefs of Western democracies
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS5K06 (Democracy, elections and representatives): Students understand democratic values, electoral features and the roles of elected representatives. From AC9HS6K01 (Federation and democracy): Students understand how Federation established Australia's constitutional framework.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the key institutions of Australia's system of government, how it is based on the Westminster system, and the key values and beliefs of Western democracies.

nodes.label: Key institutions: monarchy, parliament and courts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the roles of the key institutions of Australia's system of government: the monarchy and its representatives, parliaments, and courts.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain the role of two key institutions in Australia's system of government.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the role of the monarchy and its representatives in Australia (including the Governor-General), the parliaments (Commonwealth and State/Territory), and the courts, as the three key institutional pillars of Australia's system of government.
wider: Investigate Parliament House and the High Court in Canberra (virtually or in situ) and explain how the physical design of these institutions reflects their roles in the democratic system
Explore a recent case where the judiciary has exercised its independence from parliament or the executive, and explain what this reveals about the role of courts in Australian democracy
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish the key institutional actors (monarchy/Governor-General, parliament, courts) will conflate the roles of different branches of government and cannot understand the separation of powers that underpins Westminster-style democracy.

response_modes.reason: Use an institutional roles framework (who they are / what they do / why they matter) for each institution before moving to how the Westminster system connects them.

success_criteria: Students identify at least three key institutions and explain the role of each.
Students distinguish the roles of the parliament, the monarchy/Governor-General, and the courts.

nodes.label: Australia and the Westminster system
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare Australia's system of government with the Westminster system, identifying similarities and differences between the Australian Parliament and the UK Parliament.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe two similarities and one difference between Australia's parliament and the Westminster system.
nodes.typical_width: Compare Australia's system of government with the Westminster system: explain that the House of Representatives and Senate parallel the House of Commons and House of Lords, but that the Australian Senate has elected members (unlike the UK Lords); describe the common features of constitutional monarchy, responsible government and parliamentary sovereignty.
wider: Investigate how Australia's constitutional development has modified the Westminster model to create a distinctively Australian hybrid system
Explore how bills move through the Australian parliament, including the role of parliamentary committees and public submissions — and compare this process with the Westminster equivalent

response_modes.reason: The comparison requires students to hold two systems simultaneously — use a structured comparison table before asking for an integrated explanation.

success_criteria: Students identify at least two similarities between Australia's parliament and the Westminster system.
Students identify at least one significant difference (e.g. elected Senate).

nodes.label: Values of Western democracies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the key values and beliefs of Western democracies — including freedom of speech, equality before the law, social justice, and the rule of law — and trace their origins.
nodes.minimum_width: Name two key values of Western democracies and explain what each means in practice.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the key values of Western democracies: freedom of speech, equality before the law, social justice, and the rule of law; trace their origins in British and European democratic traditions (France, USA); explain how these values are reflected in Australian law and government.
wider: Investigate the influence of French and American democratic traditions on Australian constitutional values and identify specific features in Australian law that reflect these influences
Explore a current challenge to democratic values in Australia or another Western democracy and assess how institutions and citizens are responding to protect those values

response_modes.reason: Democratic values are abstract without concrete examples — students need to see each value instantiated in specific laws, events and institutions to understand what the value requires and protects.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The international origins of Australian democratic values (France, USA, UK) is an elaboration-supported direction that connects constitutional history with political philosophy — tracing these origins adds genuine intellectual depth.
success_criteria: Students name at least two values of Western democracies and explain what each means.
Students give one example of how each value is expressed in Australian law or institutions.

nodes.label: How Australia's government reflects its Westminster origins and democratic values
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the key institutions of Australia's system of government, how it is based on the Westminster system, and how the system reflects key values of Western democracies.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain two key institutions, identify one Westminster connection, and name one democratic value that the system upholds.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the key institutions of Australia's government; describe how the system is based on the Westminster system; identify the key values of Western democracies that the system reflects; and connect institutional design to value protection (e.g. how the judiciary's independence protects rule of law).
wider: Evaluate how effectively Australia's system of government upholds the values of Western democracy, identifying any gaps or tensions between the ideals and the practice
Investigate the role of the Executive in relation to policy development and legislation, and assess how the Executive's relationship to parliament reflects Westminster principles

response_modes.reason: The integration challenge is connecting institutional design, historical origins (Westminster), and democratic values into a coherent account. Use a structured framework that maps each institution to a democratic value it protects.

success_criteria: Students explain at least two key institutions and their roles.
Students identify at least one Westminster feature of Australia's system.
Students connect at least one institutional feature to a democratic value it protects.
